cues.en: Hello, Brains! Who here has had a really hard time with something that should be really easy? Yeah, apparently there's a reason for that. I met Brendan Mahan at the International Conference on ADHD last year, and he had the best explanation for why simple things can be so difficult that I have ever heard. And it's a metaphor. I really like metaphors. He explained it like this. When we do a simple task, like, say, make a phone call,
cues.zh: 大家好，聪明的脑友们！你们有谁曾在本该轻而易举的事情上卡过壳？对吧，显然这背后是有原因的。去年我在国际 ADHD 大会上认识了 Brendan Mahan，关于简单的事为什么会这么难，他给出了我听过最好的解释。而且这是一个隐喻。我真的很喜欢隐喻。他是这么解释的：当我们做一件简单的事，比如打个电话，

cues.en: We're not just dealing with that task. We're also dealing with the wall of awful in front of it. We can't see this wall because it's not a physical barrier. It's an emotional one. But it's just as real and it's just as in our way. How does this wall of awful get built? According to Brendan, failure. Every time we fail at a task, we get a failure brick.
cues.zh: 我们要应付的不仅是那件事本身，还有挡在它前面的那堵“糟糕之墙”。我们看不到这堵墙，因为它不是物理障碍，而是一种情绪障碍。但它同样真实存在，同样挡着我们的去路。这堵糟糕之墙是怎么砌起来的呢？按 Brendan 的说法，是失败。每次我们搞砸一件事，就会砌上一块失败砖。

cues.en: And with that failure brick comes the disappointment brick. But we don't usually only disappoint ourselves when we fail, we disappoint others around us too. So for everyone we disappoint, or even think we've disappointed, we get an extra disappointment brick. If that disappointment results in rejection, we get a rejection brick. If we're worried that disappointment will result in rejection, we get a rejection brick. And a worry brick.
cues.zh: 伴随失败砖而来的，是失望砖。但失败时我们通常不仅让自己失望，还会让身边的人失望。所以每让我们失望一个人，甚至只是我们以为让他们失望了，就会再多加一块失望砖。要是这种失望引来了拒绝，就会多一块拒绝砖。要是我们担心这种失望会引来拒绝，也会多一块拒绝砖，外加一块担忧砖。

cues.en: Eventually, all these different bricks pile up to become a significant emotional barrier to doing that task again. A wall of awful. Everyone has a wall of awful. In fact, we all have a bunch of them. But those of us with ADHD tend to have extra, and they also tend to be bigger. Kind of like the one I have around this past-due parking ticket. Thankfully, Brendan's here to tell us what to do about these walls. Hi, what do I do about this wall? That's a big wall.
cues.zh: 最后，所有这些砖头堆积如山，成了我们再次去做那件事时巨大的情绪阻碍。一堵糟糕之墙。每个人都有一堵糟糕之墙。其实我们都有好几堵。但我们这些 ADHD 患者的墙往往更多，而且通常也更厚大。就像我为这张逾期停车罚单筑起的那堵墙一样。幸好，Brendan 今天来教我们该怎么对付这些墙了。嗨，我拿这堵墙怎么办好？这堵墙可真够大的。

cues.en: Yeah, I'm proud of it. It took me a long time to build. Okay, so we need to get to the other side of it to do the thing. Or I could just not do it. No, doing it is a good plan. So there are five ways people try to get past the wall of office. Two don't work. Three of them work, but one of those is totally unhealthy and not a good plan. The two that don't work are staring at it, sort of like we're doing right now, and going around it.
cues.zh: 是啊，我还挺自豪的，花了我好长时间才砌好呢。好，那为了把事做成，我们得翻到墙那边去。或者我干脆就不做了。不，做完才是个好办法。人们通常有五种方式试图越过这堵糟糕之墙。有两种没用。有三种管用，但其中一种极其不健康，算不上好主意。两种没用的方式是：干瞪着它，就像我们现在这样；还有绕过去。

cues.en: So staring at it doesn't engage in the wall in any way, and it's not useful. Going around it, it's just not possible. Why can't I go around the wall? Because it's a metaphor, and it's infinitely wide. I know, because I made it up. The first way that works to get us past the wall is we can turn green, we can get some purple pants, we can get really mad, and we can Hulk smash our way through this wall. But that also means we have to get really angry, and that anger damages our relationship.
cues.zh: 干瞪着它根本不会触碰到墙，毫无用处。绕过去则是根本不可能的。为什么我不能绕过去？因为这是个隐喻，它无限宽。我最清楚了，因为这是我编出来的。第一种能帮我们越过墙的方法，就是我们可以变绿、穿上紫裤子、大发雷霆，然后像绿巨人浩克一样把墙砸个稀巴烂。但这也意味着我们必须变得极度愤怒，而这种愤怒会破坏我们的人际关系。

cues.en: Because we might turn to our friend and be like, fine, I'll do the dishes. God, just shut up about it. And now I'm hurting that relationship. I mean, I got past my wall of awful for the dishes, but it's not healthy. The other option is to Hulk smash inwardly, which is when we start thinking about how much we suck and wondering, why can't I just do this? What's wrong with me? That kind of stuff. That self-flagellation eventually gives us the energy to push through the wall. But that damages our self-esteem. It's hurting our relationship with ourself. So Hulk smash is not a good plan.
cues.zh: 因为我们可能会冲朋友发火：“行行行，我去洗碗还不行吗，求你别念叨了！”这就伤了感情。我是为了洗碗跨过了“心墙”，但这种方式很不健康。另一种选择是对内施加暴力，也就是开始觉得自己一无是处，心想：“为什么我连这都做不好？我到底有什么毛病？”诸如此类。这种自我鞭笞最终能逼我们冲破心墙，但这会损伤自尊，破坏我们和自己的关系。所以硬碰硬的“浩克狂暴模式”绝不是个好办法。

cues.en: By the way, Hulk smash going around and staring at it is the body's stress response. It's fight, flight and freeze. So those are sort of our least skilled approaches to the wall of awful. And they're also the ones that are the most sort of instinctive. We can get past the wall in healthier ways. So how do we deal with this wall then in a healthy way? One of the ways to deal with it is to climb it. And that looks like staring at it to the outside observer.
cues.zh: 顺便提一句，硬砸、绕道走、干瞪眼，其实就是身体的应激反应：战、逃、僵。这些可以说是我们应对“心墙”时最笨拙的方法，却也是最本能的反应。我们可以用更健康的方式跨过这道墙。那么，到底该怎么健康地应对它呢？其中一种方法就是“翻越心墙”，这在局外人看来，往往跟“干瞪眼”没什么两样。

cues.en: Because often when we're climbing our walls, what we're really doing is a whole lot of emotional work that takes place inside of us. So we're sitting with the dread and we're talking to ourselves in our head. I can do this. Like I need to just start this. So it's like gearing up to do the thing. Yeah, that's a good way to think about it. And we're just sometimes we're just waiting for that energy to come back. Right. Sometimes we're mentally exhausted and we need a little bit of time to recharge. How can you tell if someone is staring at the wall or climbing the wall?
cues.zh: 因为我们翻墙时，内心里其实正在经历剧烈的情绪拉扯。我们一边承受着恐惧，一边在心里给自己打气：“我能做到的，我必须马上开始。”所以这就像是在为行动做准备，对，这样理解很贴切。有时候我们只是在等精力恢复，没错，有时我们心力交瘁，需要一点时间充充电。那怎么才能看出一个人是在对着墙干瞪眼，还是正在翻墙呢？

cues.en: Often we can't, you have to ask, but sometimes if we pay close enough attention, we can tell. And a good example of that is a kid who takes 20 minutes to get their binders out of their backpack. The kid is taking forever to get their binders out. The parent goes over, grabs the binder, puts it on the table, flips it open and is like, there you go, do your homework. And typically what happens then is the kid snaps and they either start yelling at mom or dad or the hood goes up and they start beating themselves up and they shut down. The kid was climbing their wall.
cues.zh: 通常很难看出来，你得去问；但有时只要仔细观察，也是能发现端倪的。一个典型的例子就是，孩子花了二十分钟才把活页夹从书包里拿出来。孩子磨蹭了半天，家长走过去一把拽出活页夹，啪地扔在桌上翻开说：“拿出来了，赶紧写作业吧。”这时孩子通常就崩溃了，要么开始冲爸妈大吼，要么拉起兜帽开始自责、彻底封闭自己。其实，孩子刚才正在努力翻墙呢。

cues.en: The reason it was taking them so long to get their binders out of their backpack was that that action was the physical manifestation of them climbing the wall. But the climb was hard and it was slow and it was taking 20 minutes. And when mom or dad insists that they do the work right now, they're saying, get to the other side of the wall. And the only option that kid has to get to the other side that quickly is to Hulk smash their way through the wall. But if we notice that someone is kind of heading towards doing the thing that they need to do,
cues.zh: 他们之所以磨磨蹭蹭拿不出活页夹，是因为这个动作正是他们“翻墙”的肢体表现。只是这堵墙太难翻、太漫长，足足花了二十分钟。而当爸妈催促他们必须立刻动笔时，就相当于在要求他们瞬间跨过去；孩子唯一能在瞬间翻墙的方法，就只剩用“狂暴模式”硬砸过去了。但如果我们发现有人已经在朝着该做的事慢慢前进了，

cues.en: Probably they're heading towards doing that thing. They just need a little bit of a longer runway. What gets tricky is when it's computer based because sometimes we do the computer equivalent of picking up sticks in the yard before we mow, but then we get sucked down the Facebook rabbit hole or whatever it is that we get distracted by. And we don't realize that we've been diverted and we're going somewhere else. So that's where an outside observer can be beneficial. They just have to be careful about how they communicate that with us.
cues.zh: 他们大概率是想去做的，只是需要一段更长的起跑跑道。比较棘手的是在电脑上做事的时候，因为我们有时会做一些类似于“除草前在院里捡树枝”的准备工作，结果却陷入了浏览 Facebook 这类事情的无底洞，被分了心。而我们甚至都没意识到自己已经跑偏了。这时局外人的提醒就能帮上忙，只是他们得讲究一下沟通的方式。

cues.en: How can I tell if I'm climbing the wall or if I'm just staring at it? Yeah!
cues.zh: 我该怎么知道自己是在翻越心墙，还是只是在干瞪着它呢？对啊！

cues.en: That's a good question. One, you have to know that you have a wall of awful for the thing that you're about to start. And if you're trying to start a task that you have a wall of awful for, as soon as you realize you're struggling, you can think, oh, I'm climbing the wall of awful. And that's the language we want to use because we could say that we are sitting with the dread, but sitting and procrastinating are very stationary verbs. Climbing is an active verb. Climbing the wall and that little reframe can help us move forward towards the task that we want to engage in.
cues.zh: 问得好。首先，你得意识到自己面对即将开始的事情正有一堵“可怕之墙”。如果你正试着开始一项让你望而生畏的任务，一旦意识到自己正陷入挣扎，你就可以想：“噢，我正在翻越这堵可怕之墙呢。”这正是我们应该用的措辞，因为我们本来也可以说自己是在“伴随着恐惧枯坐”，但“坐着”和“拖延”都是非常静止的动词。“翻越”则是一个主动动词。翻越高墙，哪怕只是这一点小小的视角转变，都能帮我们迈步向前，去投入到真正想做的事情中。

cues.en: You are doing work even though it looks like you're not. It's just emotional work. You're climbing the wall. That's it for this week. Thank you so much to our Brain Advocates and all our Patreon Brains for allowing me to continue to climb these walls. Everything I do for this tribe, I get to do because of you. Like, subscribe, click all the things so you don't miss part two, and I will see you next time. Bye, Brains!
cues.zh: 即便看起来没在做事，其实你也在付出努力，只是那是情绪上的消耗。你正在翻越高墙。本周的内容就到这里。非常感谢我们的 Brain Advocates 和所有 Patreon Brains 赞助者，是你们让我能够继续翻越这些高墙。我为这个社群所做的一切，都因你们而成为可能。点赞、订阅，把所有按钮都点一遍，这样就不会错过第二部分啦，我们下期见。拜拜，Brains！
